summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions that apply on the island.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Article 1:221 of the Criminal Code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory ground of protection against discrimination in Aruba.

On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognise same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba.

On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba passed a civil-code amendment opening registered unions to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5, with four abstentions, after a 2.5-year campaign sponsored by openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes and an Igualdad Aruba petition of nearly 20,000 signatures. The amendment extends the marriage articles of the civil code to those registered unions and grants spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024.

Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. The Associated Press reported that religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time.

Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge of 2004 to 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered.

The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

GlobalGayz describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and notes that same-sex adoption is legal. Several gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba; the last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'
tangentialFactors:
Aruba is frequently described as one of the Caribbean's most LGBT-friendly islands, and the Associated Press noted that at the time of the 2016 vote neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed same-sex unions. That comparison concerns sexual-orientation rights; it does not establish any differential treatment of trans visitors, and Aruba's anti-discrimination statute still omits gender identity.

The Kingdom-level endorsement of 22 April 2015 expressly named transgender persons among those due equal rights, but it is a statement of intent by Kingdom governments rather than an enforceable provision in Aruba's Criminal Code. The gap between that endorsement and the sexual-orientation-only wording of Articles 1:221, 2:61 and 2:62 is unresolved in the sources.

Public hostility documented on the island has been directed at visible same-sex couples rather than at trans people specifically. The Oduber-Lamer harassment of 2004 to 2007 and the Catholic Church's role in opposing the 2016 amendment indicate that visibility, not legal status alone, has driven risk.
localsOnly:
Aruba's own representation at the 22 April 2015 Kingdom endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered. That statement is a local admission about resident conditions, not a visitor-facing finding.

Residents who are read as gender-nonconforming have no enumerated ground of protection under Articles 1:221, 2:61 and 2:62 of the Criminal Code, which name sexual orientation only. Local advocacy organisations, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba, operate on the island, but the sources do not document any of them providing trans-specific legal representation.

Same-sex adoption is legal in Aruba, and registered unions open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples have been available since the 8 September 2016 vote. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, before the 12 July 2024 Supreme Court ruling made same-sex marriage legal.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents airport or border screening practice in Aruba that treats binders, packers, breast forms or gender presentation differently from other travellers, and no source addresses gender markers on passports or identity documents as issued or read in Aruba. Whether Aruban authorities inspect or question documents whose gender marker does not match the holder's presentation is unresolved.

No source addresses access to gender-affirming healthcare, hormone prescriptions or their customs treatment for visitors, and none addresses bathroom or facility access rules on the island. These remain not sourced rather than absent.

No source records any hate-crime or violence incident in Aruba against a trans person specifically. The documented harassment (the Oduber-Lamer case, 2004 to 2007) concerns a same-sex couple; whether comparable conduct against a trans resident or visitor would be prosecuted is unresolved.

The 22 April 2015 Kingdom endorsement naming transgender persons is a political statement by Kingdom governments. Whether it has been implemented in Aruban statute or practice is not sourced here.
